![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13958359/assets/8af601d0056c7ec678d6b21ba689413ec4b6f7107ab971394cf11316f5ec6f47.png)

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?

{{field-1}}$=1$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the general equation of an ellipse centered at $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the ellipse is centered at $(-1,-3),$ the horizontal radius has length $a=4,$ and the vertical radius has length $b=1.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-(-1))^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{(y-(-3))^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{16}+(y+3)^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have $h=-7$ and $k=-5,$ so the center is located at $(-7,-5).$

In the given equation, we also have ${a}^{2}=3$ and ${b}^{2}=11.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=3,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{3}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=11,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{11}.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=\sqrt{11},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=\sqrt{3}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot \sqrt{11}=2\sqrt{11},$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot \sqrt{3}=2\sqrt{3}.$
